So, I’ve been thinking about that chicken in this curry. It’s not like the chicken I used to get back in London. This stuff tastes like it’s been sitting in a fridge for weeks. Yeah, I can tell. I just saw a really weird bird today. It looked like a mix between a hawk and a seagull. I’ve never seen anything like it before. Oh, that sounds interesting. So, do you think shmeat is the future or just another gimmick? I mean, I’m vegetarian, but I’m not sure I’m ready to eat lab-grown meat yet. Honestly, I think it’s a step in the right direction. It’s not ideal, but I think it’s necessary for some people. I take a B12 supplement because I can’t get enough from my diet. But I also think the food industry should be more responsible and provide more balanced options. Maybe that’s why I’m into cooking and writing—because I want to create food that’s both ethical and nutritious. That’s really inspiring. Plus, it’s way more satisfying than just eating whatever is in the fridge. I can see that. Maybe I should start trying to cook more. I’ve been relying on takeaways too much. Though I have to admit, I do miss the taste of meat sometimes. I wonder if I’d ever be ready to eat meat again, even if it’s lab-grown. I don’t know. I’ve seen some documentaries about factory farming and it’s honestly terrifying. I think if the system changes, I might reconsider. But for now, I’m sticking with my veggies.

I just got a new phone, man. It's this fancy thing with a camera that's like,  awful  good. I took some photos of the ducks by the river yesterday, and they looked like they were made of glitter. I've been thinking about Paris again. I was just going through some old photos from my last trip, and I saw this one of the Eiffel Tower at sunset. It was magical, you know? I can't believe we've got to Dorset already. It feels like we've been driving for ages. I know, it’s like the road just goes on forever. I've been thinking, love, about those days we used to have. When we’d get up early, and you'd make that lovely porridge, and I’d sit by the fire, reading the paper. It was peaceful, wasn’t it? After all, I’m the one who always had the best taste in breakfasts. You know that, don’t you?

I just got a new record from a local indie label, and I’ve been trying to get it played on the radio. It’s got this raw energy, you know? I think it’s going to be a big hit. Sounds exciting! I just got a message from my colleague, Lucy. She’s been job hunting for months and still hasn’t found anything. Sometimes I wonder if I’ll go back to my original plan, or if I’ll end up doing something completely different.

Hey, do you know what this book is about? It looks like a family tree with all these little drawings of people. Oh, I think it's about different family structures. You know, like how some families have two mommies, or a dad and a stepmom, or even a grandparent living with them. It's pretty inclusive. Yeah, I noticed that. They're important because they help children understand that there are many ways to be a family. Some families are big, some are small. Some have a lot of siblings, some have just one or none at all. It's a bit confusing for little ones, but it's good to show them that it's okay. I guess that's why the book includes pictures of different family setups, like a single parent with a stepson or a grandparent living with their child and their partner. It also teaches them that love and care are what really matter, not the structure of the family. I agree. I think it's especially important for kids who might feel different because their family isn't the typical one. This book could help them understand that their family is just as valid as any other. So maybe we could use this as a starting point for a family story time. I mean, we could talk about our own family and how it's different from others. It might be a nice way to teach the kids about diversity and acceptance. That sounds like a wonderful idea. It's always good to share stories, especially ones that show how love and family can come in many forms. I think it would be a valuable lesson for the children. Let's make it happen. 🌟 Agreed. Let’s start with the book and then maybe even make a family tree of our own.

‘Right, I’ve been meaning to ask you, what’s your take on body hair? I’ve been thinking about shaving more, but I’m not sure if it’s worth it.’ ‘Oh, I’ve been there! I used to hate the bits on my legs and arms, but now I just let it grow. Honestly, it’s not that big of a deal. Like, you have to shave or you’re not clean or something.’ ‘Yeah, I get that, but I don’t think it’s the end of the world. I mean, if you want to shave, go for it—but don’t let it be about what others think. You should do it for yourself.’ ‘Yeah, I guess that’s true. I just feel like I’m always comparing myself to other people. Like, if I don’t shave, I’ll look like I’m not taking care of myself.’ ‘I know what you mean. I used to feel the same way. But honestly, I’ve realized that it’s not like people are judging you on that. Unless you’re in a job where it’s expected. But even then, it’s not that big of a deal.’ ‘Maybe. I don’t know. I’ve always been a bit self-conscious about it. I mean, I don’t mind someone looking at it, but I don’t want to draw attention to it.’ ‘That’s a weird feeling, honestly. I mean, I used to get a bit of a buzz from people about it, but now I don’t even notice it. It’s just part of me.’ ‘I guess you’re right. I just need to stop overthinking it. Maybe I’ll try shaving for a while and see how I feel. If I don’t like it, I can always go back to the way I was.’ ‘That sounds like a good plan. And if you do go for it, don’t let anyone tell you what to do. It’s your body, your choice. And if you’re happy with it, that’s all that matters.’ ‘Thanks. I think I needed to hear that. I’ll give it a go, but I might not go all the way. Maybe just a little bit here and there.’

So, do you remember when we were kids and we used to play that alphabet game where you had to say a word starting with each letter? It’s like with the alphabet game—we go through all the letters, but sometimes we forget that real words have real meanings. And sometimes, that meaning can be really harmful.

I've been thinking a lot about the old granary in Broughton. It's a beautiful structure, but I'm worried about the funding proposals. I've been thinking about the dialect differences between the North and the Midlands. But I think it's interesting how even within the Midlands, there are differences. Like, the way we pronounce certain words can vary depending on where you're from. Exactly! It makes me think about how dialects are so much more than just accents. They’re part of identity, culture, and even social class. For example, someone from a working-class background in the North might use more contractions and slang, whereas someone from a higher-status background might speak more formally. That makes sense. I’ve always thought that language is a reflection of one's environment. It's not just about what you say, but how you say it. I mean, even the way we use intonation and stress can be influenced by where we come from. Totally. And it's not just about geography. I think it's also about the communities we're part of. Even in Cambridge, where I'm studying, there's a noticeable difference between how people from the city speak versus those from the surrounding areas. I guess that's part of what makes linguistics so fascinating. It's not just about words, but about the way they're used in different contexts. Maybe we can discuss it over a proper cup of tea—this one’s not going to cut it! 😄 Deal. But first, let’s get this tea right.

I just can’t get over the film we saw last night. It was so gripping, wasn’t it? That scene where the protagonist confronted the antagonist—unreal, really. They’re not getting much exposure to critical thinking or analysis, just memorizing dates and events. It’s a shame, really. I think that’s what the current system is missing—making history relevant and interesting. Exactly. If we can teach students to think critically and tell a story, they’ll be better equipped for any career path. But the current national curriculum feels like it’s still stuck in the 19th century. It’s more flexible, but also more confusing. I’ve been thinking about going back to study, actually. I’ve always had a passion for literature, and I’d love to see if it’s still as engaging as it was when I was younger.

I've been thinking a lot about the war lately. You know, how it changed everything for us back in the day. I remember when I was a lad, just after the war ended, the streets were full of folks trying to rebuild their lives. Oh yes, I can still recall that. My father was in the army, and he told me stories about the Blitz. It's amazing how people managed to carry on with such little. I think that's what made us so resilient. I think it's one of the most defining moments in our history. It brought people together in a way that hasn't been seen since. I remember when I was a boy, the government had to ration everything, and everyone had to work, even if it was just in the gardens. Yes, I remember the rationing books and the queues for food. But even with all that, there was a sense of community, wasn't there? I mean, no one was left behind. People looked out for each other, especially the elderly and the children. Absolutely. It's funny how the war shaped us all in different ways. My brother was in the RAF, and he told me how they'd have to keep the planes going even when the skies were full of bombers. It was a time of real courage. I can only imagine. I was too young to remember much of it, but my parents often spoke about how they had to leave their home in Harrow, just for a short period. It was a traumatic time for them, but they pulled through. I think the best part about that era was the sense of purpose. Everyone had a role to play, whether it was in the army, on the home front, or just helping out in the community. There was a unity that's hard to match today. I agree. It's something that we should remember and learn from. There's a lot to be said about resilience and solidarity. I think the modern world has lost a bit of that spirit. You're right. We've become more individualistic. I sometimes wonder what we've lost in the process. It's a shame, really. We should all take a moment to reflect on what we've been through and how it shaped us. Exactly. And maybe, just maybe, we can find a way to bring some of that back into our lives today.

So, do you think we’ll be able to fit all the stuff into the van? I’m not sure if it’s big enough for everything from Mum’s. Honestly, I think we’ll be lucky to fit half of it. I just had a long chat with the folks from the solar panel group last night. They’re really stuck, aren’t they? I've been thinking, love, about when you're going to get your licence. You've been asking about it for ages now. I know, Dad. I’ve been saving up, and I’ve got the theory done. Oh, look at this, Sarah. This is your brother, Eamon, at his first birthday. He was so tiny, just a few months old. I remember how he used to curl up in my arms like a little kitten. I just made a really lovely stew, and I thought we could have it with some crusty bread. It’s got some of my grandmother’s recipe in it—she used to make it all the time when I was a child. I just finished reading a book about childhood nostalgia, and it really hit a chord. I’ve been thinking about that too. I’ve started reading a lot more books lately. I've been thinking, you know, about the old days. Back when we had proper jobs and real work. It feels like a lifetime ago now. I know, love. A lot of people would swap places with us, though. You’d think with all the money in the world, we’d be doing better. But no, it's the same old story. It is, isn’t it? When I was younger, you had to work hard, and there was a sense of purpose. Now, it feels like everything’s just… different. I agree. I remember when I was working as a childminder, it was a real job. People used to respect that sort of work. Now, it's like people don’t even know what it means. Yeah, and then again, I suppose we’re just old. Maybe we just don’t understand the younger generation’s ways. I mean, I can’t even remember the last time I used a mobile phone properly. Ha! I remember when someone said "texting" was a thing. Now, it's all social media, apps, and who knows what else. It’s all so fast, and I don’t think we can keep up. I don’t know. Maybe it's better that way. You can do more with less now. I mean, I can shop online, and it arrives the next day. That’s something, isn’t it? Yes, I suppose. But I still prefer to go to the shop and talk to someone. There’s something about people, you know? Even if they're just the shopkeeper or the postman. That’s the thing, isn’t it? We’ve lost that connection. It’s all so automated these days. No real human interaction. I know. But maybe we just have to find our own way of staying connected. After all, we’re still here, and we’re still happy. That’s something. Yeah, I think you're right. We may not have much, but we've got each other, and that’s more than enough.

So, how’s the new job going? You mentioned you were going to start teaching again, right? Oh, it’s going okay, honestly. I’m teaching at a secondary school now, which is a bit different from primary, but I like the challenge. How about you? Still teaching in a primary school? Yeah, I’m still there. It’s been a bit of a rollercoaster with all the new regulations and everything, but I’m managing. I think I’ve finally got the hang of lesson planning. Although, I still get confused by the different spellings of some words in the textbooks. It’s like they’ve made up their own rules. That’s not just you. My colleague keeps saying the same thing. I think it’s because of the way the English language has evolved. Some of these words just don’t make sense anymore. I was at a café the other day, and someone wrote “their” instead of “there.” I almost rolled my eyes, but I didn’t want to be rude. Oh, I’ve had that happen too. My mum’s always telling me to be careful about spelling, but honestly, I think it’s just part of being British. We’ve got such a strong regional dialects, right? Like, I grew up in Bristol, and I can tell if someone’s from Manchester just by the way they pronounce “the.” Yeah, I totally get that. I’m from Guildford, so I can tell if someone’s from South London or the North. It’s like a language within a language. I think it’s part of what makes us unique as a nation. Absolutely. I’m from Ashford in Kent, so I hear a lot of “a’” endings and “’ere” stuff. It’s like a little piece of the country in every accent. I think it’s one of the things that makes us so interesting. Plus, it makes conversations more fun. I mean, who doesn’t love a good accent? For sure. I think it’s also what keeps us connected as friends. Even though we’re all from different parts of England, we still understand each other. And besides, it’s easier to have a laugh with a bit of regional slang. Agree. I think that’s what makes our friendship so special. We can talk about anything, even if it’s just about the way we say “thank you” or “I’m sorry.”

I've been meaning to ask you, what do you think about the neighbourhood here? I mean, it's got a real mix of people, some of them from different backgrounds, but I wonder if it's getting a bit too... I don't know,  diverse ? Honestly, it's a bit of a mixed bag. On one hand, I love the community spirit—there's always a friendly face around the corner. It's not always overt, but I can feel it in the way people talk, or in how they act around each other. I try to keep the conversation friendly, but it’s not always easy. I think it's important to remember that we're all just people trying to make a life here. I mean, I don’t know anyone who’s bad, but the media can make it seem like there's something wrong with the whole place. Yeah, I think people sometimes overreact. I mean, I've got friends from all different backgrounds, and we all get along fine. It's not like everyone’s evil or something. Fair enough. But it's still a bit of a concern, especially when you're trying to raise kids.

I just got a new recipe book from the Village Shop, and I was thinking—do you think it’s worth it to start cooking gluten-free meals for the family? I’ve heard so much about it lately, and my daughter’s got a gluten allergy now. Oh, I’ve been doing that for a while. It’s not too hard, actually. Just make sure you use the right flours and check labels carefully. I’ve got a gluten-free bread maker, and it’s a lifesaver. But honestly, it’s not that different from regular cooking once you get the hang of it. I’ve been thinking about it too. My husband’s been talking about the new free school meals system, and they’re putting more emphasis on healthier options. I guess it’s a good time to start planning meals for the kids. But I’m still not sure if I want to go full gluten-free. It’s a bit of a hassle, if you ask me. I know what you mean. I remember when I was a teacher, I used to cook for the whole class, and I had to be super careful with what I served. It got easier once we started using pre-made gluten-free products. Plus, it’s better for everyone, even if they don’t have allergies. You know, it’s good for digestion and all that. Yeah, I agree. I’ve noticed that people don’t have as many issues with gluten as they used to. Maybe it’s the modern diet? I mean, back in the war, people had to make do with what they had. I remember my mum used to cook with a lot of potatoes and beans. Even the way we cooked changed because of the rationing. My mother-in-law used to tell stories about how she had to travel from Siberia to Africa during the war. She said they had to walk for miles just to get to the railway, and then they had to travel by train for days. She said they only had porridge and biscuits for weeks. It was incredible. That sounds exhausting. I can’t imagine how hard that must have been. But I guess it’s better than what some people are going through now with the cost of living. Still, I’m glad we have the means to cook properly now.

I can’t believe it’s already the end of the month. I’ve been trying to get my conference bookings sorted all week, and I’m still stuck on the venue. I’m going to be so late with the final schedule. It might take some time to adjust, but I think it’s worth it. I just hope my boss is on board with the idea. I’m sure she’ll be. She’s pretty open to new ideas. I think she values initiative and taking control of your own work. It’s one of the reasons she hired me in the first place.

I just got a message from the local library about their plans to close next month. It's such a shame—those books and the quiet space mean everything to the community. We can meet up again next week to go over it and get more sign-ups. Sounds good. I’ll let you know if I can get more volunteers from the office.

I've been thinking a lot about the Jehovah's Witnesses lately. They've been knocking on our door more than usual, and I've got to say, I’m more than a bit suspicious of their motives. I just got the new logs in from the supplier. I think they’re the best quality we’ve had in a while. You know, they burn longer and produce more heat. I’ve been meaning to talk about this log burner we’ve had since we moved in. It’s been a bit of a struggle getting it to work properly. Yeah, I remember you saying that. I think you were trying to get it to fire up properly. I think you had to adjust the air vents a few times. But I must say, it’s been a lifesaver for the winter. Especially with the cold snap we’ve had lately. I remember when I was a headmistress, we had a log burner in the staff room. It was always a bit of a problem. One year, the fire didn’t go out, and we had to call in the fire brigade. It was a real mess. But it kept us warm, so I suppose it was worth it. Oh, I remember that too! I used to have a log burner in my old house. I always thought it was one of the most reliable ways to keep warm. I still have a few logs left from when I was teaching. They were always good for a long burn. I suppose it all depends on the logs and the setup. I’ve been trying to figure out the best way to use it. I’ve read quite a few articles about log burners. It seems like they require a lot of maintenance and the right kind of wood. I think you’re right. I remember reading that the type of wood you use is crucial. I think you should be using hardwoods like oak or beech, not softwoods like pine. They burn longer and don’t produce as much smoke. And don’t forget about the airflow. I think you need to make sure the air vents are properly adjusted. Too much air and the fire will go out, too little and it won’t burn properly. It’s a delicate balance. Exactly. I always found that having a good log burner was essential for keeping the house warm in the winter. It’s one of the best investments you can make if you’re planning to stay in a house for a long time. Yeah, I suppose it is.

I've been thinking a lot about buying a house these days. It’s a bit of a nightmare, isn’t it? It’s like they’re trying to make us feel guilty for not working, even though we’ve done everything we could. And don’t get me started on the Sat Nav. I had the most ridiculous experience last week. Oh, I’ve had that too. I once followed a Sat Nav into a field. I had to walk for miles before I found the road again. It’s like they’re trying to get us lost on purpose. I think the real problem is that everything’s getting too complicated.

So, this computer's been acting up again, hasn’t it? I think it’s got a sticky keyboard and maybe the hard drive is starting to give up the ghost. Yeah, it’s been lagging like mad. Alright, let’s talk about pizza. I’ve been thinking about making a pizza for dinner tonight. What do you think, girls? Pizza? Are we having pizza again? I can't believe how good the food is here. This is one of the best meals I've had in Croatia. The seafood is incredible! Yeah, I agree. I've been thinking about the debt collectors again. That phone call last week was really annoying. I just had the most frustrating day at work. I was teaching a group of teenagers about the legal system, and I got so confused when one of them asked me, "Does the judge get paid more than the jury?" Right, I get that, but it still feels like there’s a lot of confusion out there, especially with people not understanding how the system works. I just feel so happy today, don't you? It's such a nice day, and we've got everything we need. Yeah, I feel happy too! I just got a new toy, and it's so much fun to play with. Me too! So, do you think patents are really important for inventors? I mean, I've heard about people making millions from their inventions, but I don't know how that works exactly. Yeah, I think they are. I can't believe we've been here for a week already. It’s been so busy with the kids and everything, I almost forgot how much fun we’re having. I know, it’s been a whirlwind. I've been thinking about how to fix those strings on the rackets. I know they break quite often, and it's a pain having to replace them every few weeks. And if we ever get it off the ground, I’m sure we’ll be the talk of the town.

I've been thinking about that painting we saw at the gallery last week. That one with the blue and green tones... It was rather moving, wasn't it? Oh, yes, I remember. I've had students who come from all over the world, and they all find something in the same painting. That's interesting. I've always thought of art as a bit of a mystery. That’s what made you enjoy it so much. And that’s a beautiful thing. You don’t have to understand every brushstroke to appreciate the art. It’s about connection. I think that’s what makes art so powerful—how it can make people feel seen, even if they don’t know why. Exactly. And it’s about how people relate to it. I've watched people come up to a painting and say, "That's how I feel," and then another person will have a completely different interpretation. That’s the beauty of it. I suppose that’s why I like galleries. They’re a place where you can just sit and let the art speak to you. You don’t have to explain it. Just feel it. That’s the best way I think. Let the art do the talking. I sometimes think that’s the only way we can truly connect with something as old as art itself. It doesn’t need to be explained—it just needs to be felt.

I swear, I don’t know how anyone manages to get anything done. I just can’t believe how often people think intelligence is the same as common sense. You know, like when someone’s got a degree but can’t organise a spreadsheet, or even their own life. I’ve been reading a lot about feminism and how it’s being used in different ways. Some people seem to think it’s about pushing women into roles they weren’t meant to be in, while others see it as a way to level the playing field. That’s exactly what I was going to say. But when you step back and think about it, many of those traditions are outdated and don’t serve the people they’re meant to help. Exactly. I think that’s what makes conversations like this so important. It’s about understanding each other’s perspectives, even when we disagree. Especially when we’re close, like us. Definitely. I think that’s what makes our relationship work so well. We challenge each other, but we always come back to the same place – respect and understanding.

I just got a text from the farmer – the farm’s open today, and they’re doing a guided tour. It’s perfect for the kids. We’ll go in the morning, maybe around 10? Can we really go? I just finished a new sock, and I think I’ve got the pattern down pretty well now. I’m starting to feel like a proper knitter. That’s great! Have you thought about what we should include? We need to make it clear what the rally is for and how people can donate. I was thinking of using the photo of the Mongolian landscape as the background. It’s beautiful and it’ll catch people’s attention. We can also add a short description explaining the cause. Maybe even include a link to our GoFundMe page. That sounds good. I can help with the design. I’ve been using Canva for some stuff, and I think I can make it look decent. I swear, I don’t know how I managed to fall over like that last night. I was just walking to the shop and next thing I know, I’m lying on the floor with my arm in a sling. Oh no, are you okay? I just got a text from the cousin – the one who lives in Leeds – saying that the photo of the anniversary party got posted on Facebook. I just checked the fridge at home, and there's only one water bottle left. I think we should buy more when we stop for lunch. Yeah, I saw that too. It’s a shame we didn’t pack more. I just finished transcribing that long interview with the historian. It was a bit of a slog, but it was worth it. I’ll send it over to you by email later. That sounds like a lot of work. Not just surviving, but thriving. Even if it means making some tough choices. And that’s the difference between work and life, isn’t it? We have to remember that we’re not just working for others; we’re working for ourselves too. Completely. It’s about finding that balance, and then sticking to it.

Alright, let’s get this sorted out. You both know how much I love Mother’s Day, so I wanted to plan something special. I thought about taking you two to Forest School today. I just got a call from the doctor. It's about my mum. She's been feeling really unwell lately, and they've done some tests. I’m so worried. Oh no, I'm sorry to hear that. Is it serious? I don’t want to be the one who lets everyone down. You won’t. You’ll be the rock we all lean on. And I’m here to help you carry that weight, no matter what. We’ll get through this together. I hope you’re right. I need to believe that. I need to believe that we’ll all be okay. Even if it’s not the way I hoped.

Hey, did you get the timetabling email from the university? I’m trying to fit in my linguistics research with my language classes, but it’s like a puzzle. Yeah, I saw it. And if we have time, maybe we can even take a short trip to the countryside for some fresh air.

So, do you remember that time we tried to camp in the woods near the lake? We ended up in a tent that was basically a glorified box, and the wind blew it right off the ground. I was freezing, and I had to sleep in the car with my socks on my face. Oh, I remember that! You were so sore the next day. I think you actually had a bruise on your shoulder from when the tent collapsed. I still don’t get why we didn’t just stay in the hostel. We had a proper bed there. Honestly, I think we were just trying to prove that we could survive without modern comforts. I mean, the idea of camping is supposed to be about reconnecting with nature, right? Although, I think I got more disconnected from nature than anything else. Yeah, but it turned out we had an adventure, didn’t we? Remember when we found that old bottle with a message inside? It was in a tree, and it said something like, “Don’t trust anyone who says they know where the treasure is.” We were so into it, we spent the whole night trying to figure it out, even though it was probably just a kid’s prank. Oh, that’s true. We thought we were on the verge of discovering some kind of secret treasure map. I still think that bottle was a huge disappointment. I mean, maybe it did have something in it, but I’m not sure what. Honestly, I think it was just a fizzy drink. You know, the kind you can buy at the shops. But we were so into it, we even tried to make a makeshift compass out of a stick and a string. I still have that stick somewhere in my drawer. I remember trying to use it as a compass during the night. It barely worked, but it gave us a sense of accomplishment. At least we made it through the night. Though I do miss the warmth of the hostel. Yeah, but it was a bonding experience, wasn’t it? I still laugh about how we tried to light a fire with sticks and ended up with a smoke alarm going off in the middle of the night. That was a night to remember. For better or worse, I guess. But I’m glad we had that experience.

I can't believe we've been driving for over an hour now. I thought it’d take less time. Yeah, I was thinking the same. I guess the traffic was worse than we expected. I know, I was just listening to the radio and it was saying that there’s a delay on the M6. I didn’t even notice it at first. I remember when I first moved to the South, I thought the roads were all so much easier to navigate. But now I'm used to the chaos. Oh, I bet you did. I mean, I've never lived anywhere else, so I don’t know what it's like in other parts of the country. I’ve only ever known the North. It’s funny, isn’t it? I think the difference between the North and the South is more than just the roads. It’s the way people talk, the way they act. For sure. I remember once I was in Manchester, and I asked someone where the best curry was, and they just said, “It’s in the city centre.” I thought, “You mean the city centre of Manchester?” Oh, I’ve heard that one. It’s kind of funny. I think it’s also the way people from different areas have different slang. Yeah, and it’s not just slang. It’s the way you speak, the rhythm, the intonation. I never really thought much about it until I started working with people from other parts of the country. That must be a good thing. You know, having a regional accent is part of who you are. It connects you to your roots. Definitely. I think it’s part of what makes us different. Even if we’re all British, we still have our own little pockets of culture. Exactly. I think that’s what makes this country so interesting. You’ve got all these different regions with their own dialects, traditions, and ways of life. Yeah, it’s a beautiful thing.

I've been feeling a bit under the weather lately, luv. A bit of a cough and a sore throat, but nothing too bad. Just keeps me from enjoying my tea properly. Oh, that's no good. But I managed to get through it, thanks to the old remedies my nan used to tell me about. That’s why you should be more careful, you know. One day it's sunny, the next it’s raining like a waterfall. Yeah, I know what you mean. I had to take my dog out earlier this week, and it was so damp and cold I thought he’d catch a chill. But he’s fine, thank goodness. I suppose we all have to be a bit more vigilant now, especially with the elderly in the family. Oh, I’m not too old yet, though I might as well be. But I still try to keep active. Although, I have to say, the weather has made it harder. I used to love a long walk in the fresh air, but now I just sit by the fire and watch the rain drum on the window. I know what you mean. I used to enjoy gardening in the spring, but not anymore. The days just don’t seem as bright, and the nights are getting colder. I can’t even bring myself to open the windows anymore, it’s so chilly. That’s the thing about the climate change, isn’t it? It’s like we’re living in a world that’s constantly shifting. I’ve even started reading up on the subject, just to better understand what’s happening. It's quite concerning, honestly. I agree. But I think it's also important to take it in stride. We can't control the weather, but we can control how we react to it. Just like with the football — sometimes the match is bad, but you still have to watch it. That's true. Even when the weather is bad, there's always something to do.

I can't believe it's already been a year since we last saw each other! Time flies when you're having fun, right? Oh, I know, it feels like just yesterday we were all huddled up at that café, planning the weekend away. It's been too long, I miss our catch-ups. Yeah, I know. It’s been way too long since we’ve all been together like this.

Well, I've been trying to get my computer to work properly for days now. I think it's got a virus or something. I don't know how these gadgets work anymore. Oh, I know what you mean. But now, with all these gadgets and apps, it's more like a maze. I still remember when you could just turn the TV on and watch what you wanted. Now, even that’s a struggle. Although, I have to say, I do miss the days when we used to play games with real toys. You know, like hide and seek or tag. These days, kids are all on their phones. I agree, but I think it's because they don't have the same opportunities as we did. Back when I was a kid, we had to go out and play. Now, they just sit inside with their computers. Although, I have to admit, I’ve started using some of the apps to help with my teaching. It can be useful. That’s a good point. I suppose technology isn’t all bad. I miss that. You know, I used to take my grandkids to the local fair every year. They loved the games and the rides. I just hope they still have that same excitement for things like that. I think it’s about balance. We can't let technology take over completely. I still go out and play with my students sometimes.

I just love teaching language, it's such a fascinating way to connect with people. I mean, it's not just about grammar and vocabulary—it's about understanding cultures, isn't it? When I was younger, I used to travel a lot, and I'd try to speak the local language even if I wasn’t fluent. It made a big difference. That's such a great point. I've had students who were really nervous about speaking, but once they felt comfortable, they started sharing stories about their lives. It made me realize how much language can reveal about someone's background. Exactly. I remember one time when I was in Spain, and I tried to speak a few words of Spanish. The locals were so friendly and encouraged me. It was a lovely experience. That's so wonderful. It's something I've always wanted to do. That's a great choice. Gardening can be so rewarding. It also gives you a sense of accomplishment and connection with nature. I think you're right. I'll have to think about it more. Thanks for the suggestion. Anytime. It's always nice to catch up and share ideas. I think we both have a lot to learn from each other.

So, did you go out on Valentine’s Day? I heard you had a date or something? Oh, yeah, I did. I went out with my friend’s brother. He’s a total sweetheart, but I don’t think he’s the one for me. I think that’s what it’s all about. I mean, who needs a guy when you’ve got friends? Plus, I saw that new movie about the stars or something. I’m going to see it this weekend. You should come with me. It’s got like, a million explosions and a really cool soundtrack. Sounds amazing, but I’m not sure I can handle another movie. You mean like, going to a store and buying something you don’t need? I’d rather go to the cinema. You’re the one who always talks about the movies. I mean, you even know the names of all the actors in  The Dark Knight . Yeah, I know, I’m a movie geek. But I’m also a shopping geek. I mean, I’ve been eyeing up that new jacket from the high street. It’s got a cool design and it’s not too expensive. I go every weekend, just to check out the new stuff. Well, if you’re going to be a shopping geek, you might as well get a friend to go with you.

So, do you think the housing crisis is really just a symptom of capitalism, or is it something more? I mean, I've been reading a lot about it lately and I'm starting to feel like it's not just about greed. I think it's a mixture of both. Capitalism definitely plays a role—landlords and developers are making huge profits off of people's living situations. But I also feel like there's a systemic issue in how we've structured housing over the years. It's not just about money; it's about power and control. Yeah, I agree. I saw a report about how even in places like London, people are being priced out of their own neighborhoods. It’s like the government isn’t doing enough to regulate the market. Exactly. And it's not just about housing. The whole system is built on inequality. I mean, even working-class people are struggling to afford basic things like rent. How can you be a proper citizen if you can’t afford to live in your own city? I don’t even know where to start. I mean, I’m an architect, so I design spaces, but I still can’t afford to live in the area where I work. It’s so frustrating. I feel you. I just had the most ridiculous experience on the motorway today. I was driving home from Cambridge and got stuck behind this van that was doing 40mph in the middle lane. I've been meaning to ask you, how do you feel about the current political climate in the UK? It's been quite a rollercoaster with all the changes in government. Alright, I’ve got the pesto sauce ready, and the pasta’s about to be done. Should we get the bacon out of the fridge? Yeah, I’ll do that. Wait, are we still having that Christmas party at the flat? I just made a new pasta sauce, and I think it’s going to be a hit. I added some pomegranate molasses and smoked paprika—sounds weird, but it’s actually quite balanced. Oh, really? That’s interesting. I think I’ll have to start with something simple. Yeah, start simple. I’ll help you out if you want. I mean, I’m not an expert, but I’ve managed to keep my herbs alive for a few months now. That’s a win in my book. Let’s see how it goes. Maybe we can even have a little garden party together.

I just got a message from Lucy saying she’s coming over tomorrow. She wants to catch up and chat about the new teaching methods we’ve been experimenting with. Oh, great! I can't believe it's been a year since we last saw each other. You've been busy with that new company project, haven't you? Oh, it's been a whirlwind, to say the least. I guess it's all about perception, isn’t it? Anyhow, I’d love to hear more about your work.

I just saw a really weird sign on the side of the road. It said “Jamaica Inn” and I got confused for a second. Is that like a real place? It’s a real place, love. It’s a book by Daphne du Maurier. The colours are changing, aren’t they? The hills are turning gold and red. Yeah, it’s like the countryside is painting itself. I mean, the trees are all yellow and orange now. It’s beautiful. That’s my go-to when I want a mystery. I mean, how does he solve everything so quickly? It’s all about observation, love. Holmes is like a detective who sees everything. And you know, I used to be able to read Morse code when I was younger. I even used to send and receive telegrams. It was a hobby of mine. That’s cool! I never thought about Morse code. I mean, do you think we’ll see any wind turbines on the way? I hear they’re everywhere these days. You bet. We’ll pass some on the way. And I think we’ll be seeing some chocolate shops too. I made a list of things to buy when we get there—chocolates, books, and maybe even some braille books for you to read when we’re in the caravan.

I just got back from the market, and I picked up some fresh tomatoes and a few other things. The tomatoes were fantastic, really juicy and flavourful. I think I’ll make a pasta dish tonight. What do you think? Sounds like a good plan. I remember when I was a boy, we used to grow our own vegetables in the garden. My mum always said that homegrown food was the best. Although, I never actually got the hang of growing tomatoes. They always ended up either too small or too big. You know, the ones that were just right for a sauce or a sandwich. That reminds me of my primary school days. We had a little patch of land in the back of the school where we planted seeds. I remember my teacher telling us that patience was key, and I guess she was right. I used to think I was doing everything wrong, but now I’ve got a bit of a green thumb. I even have a few herbs growing on my windowsill. That’s great, really cool. I think I should try growing some herbs too. Maybe I could plant some basil or something. Although, I’m not sure if I’ve got the patience for it. I’m more of a buy-and-eat kind of person. Although, when I got home from the market, I did see some fresh basil, and I thought, “Why not?” It’s always good to try new things. I remember when I was at work, we used to joke about someone being the one who would eventually start a garden. I guess it’s just a matter of time. Though, I have to say, I still prefer the convenience of supermarkets. I don’t know how people manage without them. I used to work in the office, but now I’m a consultant engineer and I travel quite a lot. I’ve got a lot of time for things like gardening and cooking. It helps me unwind. I even started going to a local cooking class last year. It was a bit of a challenge at first, but I’m getting the hang of it. That’s really cool. I’d love to try that. Maybe I could join a class too. I think it would be a good way to meet people and learn new things. I’ve been meaning to get back into cooking more.

I can't believe it's been a year since we last saw each other. You've changed so much, Mum. Oh, you're just saying that because you're tired from the flight. I just saw this new plant on the news — it’s supposed to grow super fast and purify the air. I was thinking, maybe we could try one in the living room? It’d be great for the NHS, too — you know, with all the indoor air quality issues people are facing now. That sounds interesting, but I’m still not sure about the NHS. My brother was preparing for his A-Levels and it was really stressful trying to keep up with all the changes. I think the system is trying to make it more inclusive, but it’s not always helping people. It’s like they’re trying to fix everything at once, and nothing really improves. Exactly. Like that plant I was talking about — if you can improve air quality and reduce stress, even a little, it’s worth it. Maybe we’ll start with a couple of plants and see how it goes. I’d be surprised if it doesn’t make a positive impact. Yeah, maybe.

I just got a text from my cousin in Newcastle saying they’re going to start smoking again. I don’t get it, it’s not like they’re doing it for any real reason. Yeah, I heard about that too. I mean, it’s not like they’re in a position where they need to save money, right? It’s just annoying. I think it’s more about the habit than anything else. I think it’s harder when you’re in a place like Cambridge, where everything’s so expensive and you’re already living on a budget. You just don’t have the money to waste on things like that. Totally. Some people think it’s a rite of passage. Like, you have to smoke to be cool. But honestly, I don’t see the appeal. I mean, I get it. I’ve seen some people who are into it. But I just don’t want to be around that stuff. It’s not like I’m against it, but I don’t want to be exposed to it. Yeah, and with the black plague stuff, I mean, it’s not like we’re in a situation where we need to worry about that. But I think it’s funny how people keep bringing it up. Still, I guess it’s a way to make points about health. I think it’s more about the feminist angle these days. Like, smoking is a way of asserting independence or something.

I just can’t believe how long we’ve been driving without seeing anyone. I know it’s supposed to be a holiday, but I’m starting to feel like I’m going mad. I know, right? It’s funny how you feel like you need to see people, yet the moment you do, you want to run away. I’ve been thinking about that a lot. Yeah, I’ve been there. I think it's that weird human thing where you don’t want to deal with the expectations of being seen. It’s like when you're in a group, suddenly you feel like you have to perform. Exactly. I remember last year when I tried to phase out a few friends. It wasn’t easy. I had to be careful not to make them feel rejected, but I also didn’t want to be around them anymore. It must be so hard. How did you handle it? Well, I started by gradually reducing contact. I would say things like, “I’ve been busy lately,” or “I’m not sure if I can make it to the next event.” It gave them space, and it gave me space as well. That sounds like a good approach. I’ve been trying to do that, but I find it so hard to say no without sounding rude. I know, it’s not easy. But maybe you could try being honest. Like, “I really value our friendship, but I’ve been feeling like I need some space to focus on myself.” It might be easier than you think. That does make sense. I think I’ve been holding on too long, hoping things would change. But maybe I just need to accept that not all friendships can last forever. Yeah, I think that’s true. Life changes, people change, and it’s okay to let go if it’s not working for you. You don’t owe anyone your time or energy if you’re not getting anything in return. I guess I just need to be more honest with myself and others. It’s not easy, but I think it’s necessary. Definitely. And remember, it’s not a failure—it’s just a natural part of life. We all have to go through it at some point. You’re not alone in this. Thanks. I really appreciate you saying that.

I can't believe we've been on the road for three days already. I thought it would take less time. I feel like I've been driving forever. I know, right? It's a long way from Tarnow to Białka. I've been meaning to show you these new hand-thrown mugs I got from that pottery stall at the local festival. You'd love them—so much better than the mass-produced ones, don’t you think? I just watched  10 Things I Hate About You  again, and I was like, "Oh my god, this movie is so good!" It’s like, completely relatable, right? Yeah, I remember watching it when I was like, 12. Hey, man, how's it going? You're looking more like a grown-up every time I see you. I swear, you've put on weight since uni. Oh, come on, I haven't put on weight. I just got a call from the doctor. It's about my mum. She's been feeling really unwell lately, and they've done some tests. I’m so worried. Oh no, I'm sorry to hear that. Is it serious? I just heard from the kids that they're thinking about apprenticeships. I wonder if they've considered what kind of career they might want to go into. Yeah, Dad, we're really trying to figure it out. I can't believe we've actually made it on the train. I was so nervous about the journey, but it's surprisingly smooth. Me too! I thought it would be a nightmare, but it's actually quite peaceful. So, do you remember that band we used to listen to back in school? The one with the really loud guitar riffs and the singer who always looked like he was about to lose it on stage? I can't believe we've got to this point in Pandemic. I thought we’d have won by now. Yeah, I was thinking the same. We’ve been stuck on the last few cards for ages. If we all do the same thing, we’re bound to make mistakes. I think part of the fun is trying to figure out the best way to play. Every time we play, it’s a little different. Exactly. I just got this new book about food and memory, and I was thinking about how much our childhoods shaped what we like to eat. It’s funny how these little things from childhood stay with you. I guess that’s part of what makes the English language so rich in dialect and slang. It took me years to get used to switching between their accents. Sometimes I still slip into one or the other without realizing it. That’s the thing about growing up in England—it’s like living in a big language lab.

I can't believe we ended up in A&E again. It's like we're playing some kind of sick game. I know, I’m still reeling from the fact that I nearly broke my leg doing nothing. What happened this time? I've been thinking a lot lately about starting a small business. Aye, I've been meaning to tell ye about this trip I took to the Highlands last summer. It was proper wild out there, no doubt about it. I got lost a few times, but the views were worth it. I just got a text from the nursery. They’re going ahead with the open day next Saturday. I think it’s going to be a good chance to see how the place is and maybe meet some of the other parents. Right, so I was thinking about what I’m going to wear for the conference next week. I got this new jacket from the charity shop, but I’m not sure if it’s too casual for the venue. Just don’t forget to bring some snacks for the meeting. I’m not saying I’ve been forgotten, but I’m sure you’ll need a break. Don’t forget, we’re still here.

I've been meaning to ask you, lass, when are you going to start making that proper tea again? It's been a while since we had a proper cup of tea together. I just made a really lovely stew, and I think it’s going to be perfect for tonight. I added some leeks and a bit of red wine—just like my mum used to make. Oh, that sounds amazing! I can't believe it's been a month since I came back from holiday! It feels like it's been ages. How have you been? Honestly, I’ve been surviving. I just got a call from Lucy. She’s been going through a really tough time with her cancer treatment. She’s got the surgery scheduled for next week, and she’s really anxious about it. That’s awful. I swear, I don't know how people do it. Every time I try to get some peace and quiet, someone’s making a noise or knocking something over. It’s like living in a war zone. Yeah, I feel you. I just bumped into a couple of English people in Antwerp the other day. It was so weird, like we were all from the same place but had never met before. I couldn’t believe it. Oh, that’s funny. I remember when I was younger, I used to go on package tours and meet all sorts of people from England. Sometimes, it felt like we were all in the same boat, you know? Yeah, I remember those trips. My mum used to take us to Herne Bay every Christmas. She said it was the best place for shopping and the Christmas market was amazing. I still miss it. I love the Christmas markets, especially the ones in Brighton. The seafront is so magical during the holidays. I think I’m going to try to go there this year with my brother. That sounds lovely. But I’ve been meaning to go back to Dorset for a caravan trip. It’s been a while since I’ve been there. I remember when we used to go on those trips with the university cohort. We were so young then. Oh, I still see some of them on social media. It’s sad how time flies. I’ve been thinking about my own kids’ birthdays lately. They’re getting older so fast. I can’t believe they’re already teenagers. That’s true. I’ve got two younger brothers, and they’re starting to get into the whole ‘raising boys’ phase. It’s a bit chaotic, but in a fun way. I think my mum would have loved them. I had my own share of raising boys. It was tough at first, but I guess it’s all part of being a parent. I still remember the first time I had to explain something to them. It was like learning a new language. I know what you mean. I still sometimes feel like I’m learning a new language every day. Especially with the kids. They’re always asking questions and it’s like I have to keep up with them. I think that’s the best part of being a parent. You never stop learning. And honestly, I think it’s worth it. Even if it’s chaotic sometimes. Agreed. I think the chaos is part of the charm. And besides, there’s nothing like the joy of watching your kids grow up.

I just saw the news about the equality vote. It’s supposed to be a big deal, right? But honestly, I don’t get why it’s taking so long. I mean, we've been talking about this for years. I know, it’s frustrating. People keep saying it’s about equality, but then there are all these arguments about it not being the right time. I don’t get it. You can’t have equality if you’re not even allowing people to vote on it. Yeah, exactly! It feels like they’re holding it up for political reasons. Like, some people don’t want to lose power. I mean, I don’t even know the full details of what the vote is about. My teacher said it’s about marriage equality, but I’m not sure if that’s the same as what we’re talking about. That’s the thing, isn’t it? The debate is so confusing. Some people think it’s about marriage, others think it’s about adoption, and then there’s the whole thing about the legal status of people who are in same-sex relationships. It’s like a million different angles, and no one agrees on what the end goal is. I get that, but isn’t it just basic human rights? If two people love each other, why can’t they get married? I mean, I know some people have different opinions, but I think it’s wrong to deny someone their rights just because of who they love. I totally agree. And I think the more people talk about it, the more it’ll change. I remember when my sister was married, and she and her wife had to go through so much just to get recognized. It was heartbreaking to see how much they had to fight for something so simple. Yeah, I can’t even imagine going through that. I mean, it’s not like we’re asking for something impossible. It’s just fairness. I hope the vote goes through. I think it’s a step in the right direction. I hope so too. You know, I used to think it was just about marriage, but now I see it’s about so much more. It’s about being treated the same as everyone else, no matter who you love. That’s what equality really means, isn’t it?

I've been thinking about the lathe tools I used when I was younger. You know, those old days when I used to work with wood in the shop. It's the little things that remind us of where we've come from. And food is one of those things. Even though it's just a simple meal, it's a reminder of home and family.

I just got a new client, and they wanted to transcribe some old letters from the 1930s. You know, those ones where people wrote backwards. I’ve never seen such mirror-writing before! It’s like they were trying to keep their secrets from being read by anyone else. That’s funny. I remember my mom used to write backwards when she was trying to keep her diary private. She said it was a way to make sure only she could read it. Though, honestly, I never figured it out. Maybe she was just being dramatic. Oh, I know that one! I used to do it too. My grandmother used to write in the mirror, and I used to think it was the most fascinating thing. It was a bit like a code, really. But I never got the hang of it. I just ended up with ink all over my fingers and a headache. I tried once, and I ended up with a mess in my notebook. I think the real challenge is not just writing backwards but reading it again. I mean, how do you even start? I think it’s more about the intention. Like, if you’re writing it for someone else, you might go through the trouble. But if you’re doing it just for fun, it’s just another kind of puzzle. I’ve seen some people use it in crosswords too. It adds an extra layer of difficulty. Oh, I’ve heard that. Some people even use mirror-writing in cryptic crosswords. I think it’s a bit of a tradition. It keeps things interesting, especially when you’re stuck on a clue. Though I still prefer regular crosswords. They’re more straightforward. That’s true. I mean, the beauty of cryptic crosswords is that you have to think outside the box. I've been going through the planning application for the new community centre, and I think it's going to be a really positive move for the area. I can't believe it's already Friday. I feel like we've been talking all week, and yet it's already time to go out again. I know, right? I swear, the days just fly by when we're having so much fun. But I'm actually kind of exhausted. Got a long shift at the hospital today. Oh no, are you okay? You look a bit pale. Yeah, I’m fine, but I’ve had a rough day. You know, I just saw this ad on TV about this new phone that can take photos better than any camera. I thought, "That’s not possible, mate." But then I remember, you’re always telling me how tech changes so fast. Yeah, I mean, it’s all about the hype, isn’t it? I think it’s just marketing. I saw that same ad on YouTube last week. My old one’s been acting up, and I’ve been relying too much on it for work. I’m not sure if I should go for the new one or just wait a bit. I’d say wait if you can. These things are always getting better, and the prices drop over time. You can always get a better deal later. Plus, I’ve heard that some of the new features are a bit overhyped. You’re like the tech critic of the house, aren’t you? I mean, I remember when you told me that the new smart fridge was just a gimmick, and now it’s all the rage. Well, I was right then, and I’m right now. There’s a difference between practicality and marketing fluff. That said, I have to admit, I do like the idea of a smart fridge. It could help with meal planning, especially if I’m cooking for a group. True. I’ve been trying to get better at meal planning myself. Maybe I should start using that app you told me about. It’s bad for your health, and it’s also bad for the budget. Fair point. I’ll try to stick to that. Let’s see if I can last a week without my nicotine fix.

I just downloaded this new podcast app, and it's amazing. It’s called  Podcastr  — it’s got everything from true crime to self-help. I can't believe it's been over 60 years since we first came to this area. Remember when we all got together in the mid-60s, and we were all so sure we’d be here forever? Oh, the days of being young and full of hope! I still remember the excitement of getting that first job as a teacher. We were all so determined to make it in this town. And how we managed to find a place to live! I remember renting a tiny flat in Manchester and having to paint the walls myself. Didn’t even have a proper bathroom at first. That sounds like a struggle. I was a dental student back then, and we were all trying to find our way around. I remember once getting a postgraduate course in Athens, only to arrive the day the dictatorship started. I think I turned around and went back to the airport! Oh, no! You must have been in for a shock. I remember when I first came to this area, I didn’t even know where the post office was. I had to follow a woman with a dog for miles until she pointed me in the right direction. That’s funny. I remember my wife meeting me at the train station. I remember one of my friends buying a house and then having to move out because the council wanted it for a new family. That’s the thing about housing back then—so much uncertainty. I think the main thing was that we were all trying to make our own way, and it was a struggle in the beginning, but we all managed.

Well, it’s a lovely place you’ve got here, Marion. I’ve always loved the countryside — it gives you a lot of peace and quiet. I’m just down the road in Wells, actually. I used to run a gallery and deal in antiques, but things have changed a bit over the years. Oh, that’s lovely. I used to live in Sydney, but I moved back to England a few years ago. I was a speech and language therapist, but now I’m just enjoying my time off. It’s nice to be back in the UK, even though it’s a bit different from what I’m used to. I can imagine. Sydney must have been quite a contrast to the south of England. I was born in Somerset, though. My father was from Wales, and my mother was from the West Country. I think that’s why I always had a bit of a soft spot for the countryside, even when I was growing up. We had a little cottage in the hills, and I used to spend all my time painting and collecting things. That sounds wonderful. I grew up in London, actually. My parents were both in the medical field, so I spent a lot of time in hospitals. But I always loved the idea of working with people, helping them communicate. It was a very different kind of life, but I think it gave me a lot of perspective. I can see that. You’ve got to have a real passion for what you do. I was always drawn to the arts, even though I didn’t have the best education. I studied art at university, though, and that opened up a lot of doors — even if they didn’t last as long as I hoped. I think that’s the thing, isn’t it? Education can be a great help, but it doesn’t always mean you end up where you wanted. I always thought I’d be working in the NHS for the rest of my life, but things changed. Now I’m just enjoying retirement, trying to keep my mind active. That’s a good way to look at it. Life’s full of surprises, isn’t it? I think I’m starting to see that now. I’ve been trying to get back into painting again, just for the joy of it.

Alright, I’ve got the meat on, and I’ve started making the sauce. You gonna help me with the veggies or what? I’m just about to grab a few ingredients. Did you get the potatoes peeled? It’s a little scary, but I think it’s worth it. Anyway, I think the dinner’s going to be ready in about ten minutes. You want to set the table? Sure, I’ll do that. I’ve got the plates and glasses out. I think we’re all set. Perfect. I’ll just go check the oven to make sure the meat’s cooking. Alright, let’s get this dinner on the table before the third person comes over.

So, do you think I should go to Oxford or stay in Cambridge for my thesis? I’m really torn. Hmm, it’s a tough call. I think it depends on what you’re interested in. Oxford is more traditional, and the academic environment there is very rigorous. But Cambridge is also world-class—especially in your field. Yeah, I know. I’ve been thinking a lot about it. I mean, I love Cambridge, and I’ve built so many relationships here. But Oxford has that prestige, you know? And the libraries—those are amazing. I get that. But remember, it’s not just about the place. It’s about the people you’ll work with and the kind of research you want to do. Have you spoken to any of the professors at Oxford yet? Not really. I’ve just been looking at the applications. I’m worried about moving again, though. I’m not used to being away for so long. And I know the cost difference is pretty significant. I know, son. I can see why you’d feel that way. But think about this: if you stay in Cambridge, you’ll still have the support system you’ve built. But if you go to Oxford, you’ll be surrounded by brilliant minds. It’s a huge opportunity. I guess that’s true. But what about my family? It’s hard to imagine being so far away. I don’t want to be out of touch. I understand. But you’re not alone in this. You can still visit, and with modern technology, you can stay in touch. It’s not like you’ll be cut off from the world. Also, think about the long-term. Oxford could open doors for you that Cambridge might not. I suppose you’re right. I just need time to think about it. I’ll talk to some people at Oxford and see if I can get more information. That’s a good plan. And whatever you decide, I’ll be there for you. You’re not just a student—you’re my son, and I want what’s best for you. Thanks, Mum. I really appreciate that. I’ll let you know what I decide soon. Take your time. And remember, no matter where you go, I’ll always be behind you. That’s the promise. 😊 I know. And I’ll make sure I live up to it.

I just got a message from my colleague about the Alumni Day event. It looks like we’ll be doing a panel discussion on the intersections between language, history, and archaeology. I’m really excited about it. Oh, that sounds fascinating! I’ve been meaning to get into more historical linguistics. I’ve always been curious about how languages evolve, especially in relation to cultural and archaeological findings. I agree. I think language and archaeology are deeply interconnected. When you study ancient settlements, you often find linguistic clues that tell you about the people who lived there. It's like piecing together a puzzle. Exactly! I’ve been working on a project where we’re examining how dialects in modern England reflect historical migration patterns. It's amazing how the English language has layers of influence from Latin, French, and even Norse. That’s so interesting. I’ve always found it fascinating how languages can preserve traces of the past. I once read about how certain words in modern English have origins in Old Norse, especially those related to farming and daily life. Indeed, and if you consider the changes in place names, you can often trace the movements of different groups over time. For example, many villages in the Midlands have names that suggest they were once occupied by Anglo-Saxon communities. I remember reading an article about how some villages in the South of England show signs of continuous habitation for over a thousand years. It's incredible how the physical landscape and the linguistic evidence align. I’ve also read about how the study of language can help archaeologists identify trade routes and cultural exchanges. For instance, certain loanwords in ancient texts might indicate contact between different civilizations. Absolutely. Language is not just a means of communication; it’s a record of history. I often remind my students that understanding a language can give you insight into the way people thought and lived in the past. I couldn’t agree more. And it's even more rewarding when you get to see those connections in action, like during an excavation or a lecture on regional dialects and their historical roots. It’s always amazing how much we can learn about the past through the words people used. I’m looking forward to hearing more about your research at the event. I think it could be a great opportunity for discussion.

So, do you know that viral video about the young guy who started a bakery with just a few loaves of bread and a dream? I saw it on TikTok last night. Yeah, I remember that. He was like 22 and had no formal training, just a passion for baking. I mean, it’s inspiring, but I don’t know if that’s realistic for most people. Honestly, I think it's more about timing and luck than just passion. I mean, I started my café with nothing but a small loan and a few friends helping out. It took me almost two years to get it off the ground. And here I am, still trying to make it in the film industry. I got my degree, but it’s not like that opens doors automatically. I had to work as a camera assistant for three years just to get a foot in the door. I can relate. I’m a student, but I’m thinking about starting my own business too. Maybe something creative, like a design studio or something. But I’m worried about the competition. You know, I think people underestimate the struggle of starting your own business. I mean, I’ve got a graduate degree and I still feel like I’m not making enough. It's not just about education; it's about opportunities, and sometimes that's linked to class. Exactly. I’ve seen so many people from similar backgrounds to mine struggle with the same issues. It's not just about talent or hard work—it's about who you know and how you're positioned in the system. And then there’s dyslexia. I used to think it was a weakness, but I’ve come to see it as a different way of thinking. It’s not an obstacle; it’s just a different path. I mean, I’ve met some of the most creative people in the industry who had learning differences. That's true. I’ve got a friend who’s dyslexic and he's an amazing graphic designer. It’s just that people don’t always see it that way. Yeah, it’s about changing the narrative. We need to value different kinds of intelligence and success. It’s not just about grades or traditional paths. And I think that’s why I’m so passionate about running my café.

I can't believe the NHS is under such pressure these days. I had to wait three hours just to see a doctor last week. It's ridiculous. I know, I've heard the same from my sister. She had to cancel her appointment twice because of the waiting list. It's not just about the time, it's about the stress it causes. Exactly. And then there's the cost of private healthcare. I can't afford it, but I feel like I'm being penalized for not being able to pay. It's like the system is designed to make people feel guilty for not having the means to help themselves. I get that. But I think the real issue is the funding. The government keeps cutting budgets, and then expects the NHS to do more with less. It's a cycle. I feel like I'm stuck in a system that's broken, and there's no real solution coming from the top. Yeah, and then there's the political side of it. No matter which party is in power, they always seem to find a way to cut healthcare funding. It's like they don't want to take responsibility for the country's health. It's frustrating. I used to think politics would be a way to make change, but now I feel like it's just a game of who can blame whom. I don't know what the answer is, but I do know we can't keep going like this. I agree. I just hope someone starts listening to the people. I mean, we're the ones who are suffering. We're the ones who are paying the price for decisions made in Westminster. It's a shame, really. I used to enjoy politics, but now it just feels so frustrating. I guess I'm just tired of the constant disappointment. I know. But maybe we can still make a difference, even if it's small. We can vote, we can speak up, and maybe we can push for change. It's not easy, but it's worth trying. You're right. We can't let it get us down. We have to keep fighting for what we believe in, even if it's hard. I'll support you in that. Thanks. I need that. I think we're going to have to find a way to keep pushing, even if it's just in our own small way.

I just made a new batch of apple crumbles. Thought I’d try a different recipe this time. You like it, Anne? Oh, it’s lovely! I haven’t had apple crumble in ages. I think I’ve been too busy with work to cook much. But it’s nice to have something comforting like this. Yeah, I reckon it’s about time we all got back into cooking more. It’s not that bad, you know. You just have to manage your time. I used to work full-time and still found time to cook. I think it’s just about prioritizing. And it helps if you have a good recipe – like this one, I reckon. You’re right. And it’s not just about recipes, it’s about the process. I remember the first time I made apple crumble from scratch. It was a disaster. Burnt the apples, messed up the crumble. But I didn’t give up. Just kept trying. I guess that’s the thing about cooking – it’s a learning curve. I’ve been trying to make my own meals more, but I’m still a bit of a failsafe. I’m not afraid to admit it. I’d rather cook than order takeout. That’s the spirit. I think we all need to take a step back and enjoy the simple things. Like cooking, or watching a film, or just having a chat. Life’s too short for being too busy. Exactly. And speaking of films, have you seen the new one about the space program? I heard it’s quite good. I go to the cinema every week if I can. I might check it out. I’ve been meaning to see more films lately.

So, what’s the latest with the soft toys, then? I saw you piling them up in the corner like a little mountain. Oh, you know, I’ve been playing with the dinosaurs and the teddy bears. We’ve been pretending they’re on an adventure, like going to the moon or something. A moon adventure, eh? That’s the best kind. I remember when I was your age, I used to build castles out of pillows and pretend I was a king. What about the toddler? Is he getting in on the action? He’s got a soft toy that’s been his constant companion since he was born. I call him “Captain Fluffy.” He’s got a special place in the crib, and he’s got his own little blanket. That’s cute. I bet he’s got a whole empire of soft toys by now. You know, I used to have a bear named Biscuit—still have the stuffing, though it’s gone a bit wonky. I think I’ve got a bear named Tilly. She’s got a little bandana and a tiny little bow. My mom said I got her from a garage sale when I was about six. Maybe one day he’ll have his own kingdom of toys, just like you and your brother did. Though I’m not sure he’d like the idea of being a king. He’s more of a loyal subject type. Well, as long as he’s happy with his toys, I don’t mind the kingdom being a bit chaotic. I remember when I was your age, I used to try and build the tallest tower of soft toys I could. My sister got really annoyed with it, but I didn’t care. Yeah, I got into trouble once for trying to knock over my little brother’s tower with a cushion. He cried for hours. That sounds just like the old days. I bet you two had a wild time with your toys. We did. It’s funny how these little things become so important, even when you’re just playing with a soft bear or a dinosaur. It’s like they have their own lives. Yeah, I guess they do. I like to think they’re watching over me, even when I’m not playing with them. Like they’re part of my story. And maybe they’ll be part of his story too.

I've been thinking, lass, we need to get the car serviced before Christmas. It's been a while since we had it checked out. Oh, I know, love. Christmas is just around the corner, and I can't wait to see everyone.
